strengths: First comprehensive study identifying and documenting MLLM vulnerability to misleading visualizations across 18 models and 17 misleader types with clear evidence (accuracy drops to random baseline)
Well-designed three-experiment structure (accuracy, consistency, correction methods) that builds coherently to establish vulnerability and test solutions
Diverse MLLM coverage including open-weight models (11), commercial models (4), and chart-specialized models (3) across 2B-38B parameters
Addition of real-world misleading visualizations dataset with manual MCQ annotations, complementing existing synthetic datasets
Nuanced comparative analysis revealing important differences between MLLM and human vulnerabilities (e.g., area encoding, dual-axis), suggesting domain-specific mitigation approaches are needed
Rigorous statistical methodology using McNemar tests and paired t-tests with appropriate significance thresholds and honest p-value reporting
Two practical inference-time methods showing meaningful improvements (15.4-19.6 pp for table-based QA, up to 13 pp for redrawing) without retraining
Transparent discussion of trade-offs, limitations, and identified bottlenecks (particularly table extraction); promise to release code and data
weaknesses: Critical bottleneck inadequately addressed: Table extraction achieves only 7.1% perfect match rate between paired visualizations, directly undermining both main correction methods; extraction errors cause up to 8.5 pp accuracy loss on non-misleading visualizations with no proposed solution

Severe trade-off in primary solution: Table-based QA improves misleading visualization accuracy by 19.6 pp but degrades non-misleading accuracy by 8.5 pp—an unacceptable asymmetric cost for practical deployment

Limited dataset sizes and class imbalance: Misleading set n=143 with truncated/inverted axes representing 46.9% of instances; several misleaders have only 1 example; Experiment 2 uses only 4 visualization pairs

Restricted evaluation scope for correction methods: Only 3 mid-sized open-weight MLLMs tested for corrections (not the 18 from Experiment 1); largest/commercial models excluded where solutions might have greatest impact

Shallow mechanistic analysis: Limited investigation of why table extraction fails so frequently, insufficient error analysis stratified by visualization type/misleader category, minimal exploration of failure modes for correction methods

Real-world performance (33.5%) primarily driven by parametric knowledge rather than robust understanding, undermining practical urgency; this advantage disappears with recent data where models lack background knowledge

Weak or ineffective correction methods: Warning-based approach requires perfect ground-truth misleader detection (upper-bound results); redrawing shows 79-80% success rates on complex charts; other methods produce negligible gains
Limited novelty in proposed methods: Solutions are straightforward applications of existing capabilities (table extraction, code generation) rather than novel algorithmic contributions
Incomplete practical guidance: No clear decision framework for when/how to apply each correction method; varying effectiveness across models limits applicability
Generalization limitations: Only multiple-choice and Likert-scale questions tested; English-only; relatively simple chart types; maps explicitly unsupported; open-ended QA generalization unclear

strengths: Addresses an important and socially relevant problem: MLLM vulnerability to misleading visualizations that could facilitate disinformation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 18 diverse MLLMs and 17 types of misleaders with proper statistical testing
Interesting comparative insights showing that some misleaders affect humans and MLLMs differently (e.g., area encoding), suggesting different mitigation strategies are needed
Introduces first real-world misleading visualization dataset (42 instances) and manually creates questions to enable evaluation beyond synthetic data
Honest reporting of trade-offs: transparently shows that table-based QA degrades non-misleading visualization performance by up to 8.5 pp
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective motivating examples and visualizations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core findings are not surprising and concurrent work (Bendeck & Stasko 2025, Pandey & Ottley 2025, Chen et al. 2025) reaches similar conclusions, reducing contribution distinctiveness

Proposed solutions are weak and inadequate: table-based QA (most effective) reduces accuracy on non-misleading visualizations by up to 8.5 pp, while redrawing shows modest improvements; no practical solution emerges that both solves the problem and preserves baseline performance

Critical unresolved bottleneck: table extraction achieves only 7.1% perfect match and 23-25% partial match between paired visualizations; since both most-effective correction methods depend on reliable extraction, this fundamental limitation undermines the proposed approaches

Severe scope limitation for correction methods: only 3 of 18 models evaluated, and critically, not the strongest/most-vulnerable models (GPT4o, Gemini-1.5-pro, InternVL2.5-38B); correction methods should prioritize vulnerable models yet aren't tested on them

Dataset imbalances not adequately mitigated: truncated and inverted axes comprise 47 of 143 misleading instances; 5 misleader types have only 1-3 examples; real-world subset is tiny (42 instances) with manually created questions and no inter-annotator agreement reporting

Weak consistency evaluation (Experiment 2): only 4 visualization pairs tested with only 3 distinct misleaders; results are mixed (significant inconsistency for truncated axis only, not for other misleaders), limiting ability to generalize consistency claims

Missing critical analysis: no error breakdown of which methods fail on which misleader types, no explanation of failure modes, no ablations on impact of extraction quality, and limited analysis of why performance is better on real-world visualizations (suggests problem is worse for newer data)

Incomplete methodological transparency: actual prompts for table/axes extraction not shown, real-world question creation methodology not detailed, no inter-annotator agreement for manual question creation, and how misleader warnings are generated unclear

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem—MLLM vulnerability to misleading visualizations—with clear societal implications for disinformation and public discourse
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 18 diverse MLLMs (2-38B parameters, multiple architectures), 17 misleader types, and multiple datasets combining real-world and synthetic visualizations
Rigorous methodology with appropriate statistical testing (McNemar, paired t-tests), clear experimental design, and human performance baselines for comparison
Introduces real-world dataset of 42 misleading visualizations, addressing a gap in existing benchmarks and enabling evaluation on authentic examples

Effective analysis of failure modes: identifies table extraction as critical bottleneck (7.1% perfect accuracy), reveals misleader-specific vulnerabilities differing from humans (e.g., area encoding 5.6% vs. human 91.5%)
Practical inference-time correction methods requiring no retraining; table-based QA and visualization redrawing show meaningful improvements (15.4-19.6 pp)
Well-written with clear motivation, effective examples using sensitive topics, logical organization, and honest limitations section; commits to releasing code and data
weaknesses: Solutions come with unresolved trade-offs: most effective method (table-based QA) reduces accuracy on non-misleading visualizations by up to 8.5 pp, limiting practical deployment and lacking clear guidance on when to apply which approach

Table extraction remains a critical unresolved bottleneck: only 7.1% perfect match rate on CHARTOM pairs, directly causes performance degradation on non-misleading cases, yet both effective correction methods depend on it

Limited dataset scale and severely imbalanced misleader representation: 143 misleading/124 non-misleading instances with truncated/inverted axes comprising 47/143 (33%); Experiment 2 uses only 4 visualization pairs for consistency claims
Correction methods evaluated on only 3 models despite comprehensive evaluation of 18 MLLMs; missing analysis of whether methods scale to larger models (GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-pro)

Shallow mechanistic understanding: limited analysis of why specific misleaders fool MLLMs differently than humans; parametric knowledge hypothesis for real-world data underdeveloped and unsupported; warning messages fail without clear explanation

Incomplete solution to core vulnerability: MLLM accuracy remains at random baseline (25.6%) for misleading visualizations; no training-time or deep learning-based approaches explored; only preliminary inference-time fixes proposed

Inconsistent findings reduce generalizability: model rankings vary dramatically across datasets (best on CALVI ranks worst on ChartQA); real-world performance advantage likely due to parametric knowledge rather than robustness, limiting applicability to truly novel data

Reproducibility concerns: different APIs used for different models (Azure, Google Cloud), zero-shot setup may not be optimal, limited hyperparameter specification, no ablation studies on prompt design

strengths: Identifies and comprehensively evaluates an important, previously under-studied vulnerability in MLLMs with clear societal implications for misinformation

Extensive empirical evaluation across 19 MLLMs, 17 types of misleaders, and 267 visualizations (143 misleading + 124 non-misleading + 2500 ChartQA), with multiple evaluation lenses (accuracy, consistency, error analysis)
Rigorous methodology with appropriate statistical tests (McNemar, paired t-test), multiple experiments, and detailed qualitative error analysis by misleader type (Appendices G-I)

Thorough investigation of failure modes: table extraction bottleneck identified with per-misleader accuracy analysis; only 7.1% perfect extraction match on CHARTOM pairs; honest reporting of trade-offs (8.5 pp drops on non-misleading visualizations)
Creation of new real-world misleading visualization dataset (42 instances) and promised code/data release for reproducibility
Clear practical guidance identifying which methods work (table-based QA: +15.4-19.6 pp; redrawing: modest gains) vs. ineffective (warnings, axes-only) with systematic comparison across six methods
weaknesses: Small, severely imbalanced datasets limit generalization: 143 misleading visualizations with 14 misleaders having ≤6 instances (pie charts, missing data, overplotting: 1 each); real-world dataset only 42 instances; non-misleading set also small (124)

Proposed solutions incomplete with significant trade-offs: table-based QA degrades non-misleading performance (8.5 pp); visualization redrawing has cascading failures (0% table extraction accuracy for dual axis, 8.3% for 3D); falls back to original misleading visualization when code fails

Limited technical novelty: table-based QA repurposed from Liu et al. (2023a,b) already known to be less effective than image-based methods; visualization redrawing relates to existing visualization linters; warning method performs poorly and acknowledged as 'unpromising'

Incomplete analysis of human-MLLM differences despite noting they require different mitigation strategies: some misleaders affect humans and MLLMs differently (area encoding: 91.5% human vs. low MLLM; dual axis: 16.1% human vs. 35.5% MLLM), but root causes unexplored

Parametric knowledge confound: large models (Claude, GPT4o) perform much better on real-world data (34.7% vs. 22-24% synthetic); Appendix C shows 50% accuracy on real-world MCQs without visualizations; makes isolating MLLM robustness from knowledge difficult

Experimental design limitations: Experiment 2 uses only 8 instances from single source with significance only on 2/4 pairs; Experiment 3 evaluates only 3 models not full set of 19; manual error analysis on small samples (30/143-267 visualizations) without inter-rater reliability

Statistical and methodological concerns: no multiple comparisons correction despite testing 6 methods × 19 models; effect sizes not consistently reported; mixed question types (MCQ/free-text/rank) with unclear breakdown in Experiment 3

Limited investigation of causal mechanisms: paper shows WHAT happens but not WHY MLLMs fail (visual processing vs. reasoning?); no exploration of whether fine-tuning or training data could help; limited analysis of whether table extraction accuracy is the root cause

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem with clear real-world implications for misinformation and reliability of deployed systems
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 19 diverse MLLMs, multiple datasets (synthetic and real-world), 17 misleader types, comparison with human performance
Rigorous methodology with proper statistical testing, multiple experiments assessing both accuracy and consistency, and extensive qualitative analyses of failure modes
Thorough documentation of the vulnerability across model sizes, providing valuable empirical evidence that this is not a niche failure mode
Well-written and clear presentation with detailed appendices enabling reproducibility; code and data promised for release
weaknesses: Core circular dependency undermines solutions: both effective methods (table-based QA, redrawing) depend on accurate table extraction, which itself fails catastrophically on the very misleaders they target (0% for dual axis, 8.3% for 3D effects, 15.4% for inverted axis). This creates a fundamental logical problem not resolved in the paper

Limited novelty in proposed methods: table-based QA and visualization redrawing are applications of existing techniques (Liu et al., 2023a,b); the warning method performs poorly despite ground-truth misleader information, suggesting the approach is fundamentally limited

Significant unresolved trade-offs: table-based QA reduces performance on non-misleading visualizations by up to 8.5 pp; no principled approach provided for when to apply which method, limiting practical utility

Small and imbalanced dataset (143 misleading visualizations vs 2500 for ChartQA); truncated/inverted axes dominate; some misleaders have only 1 example; limits generalization and confidence in results

Limited analysis of root causes: paper documents that MLLMs fail but provides insufficient insight into why, what visual features drive the failures, or why differential vulnerabilities exist relative to humans; this understanding would enable better solutions

Unresolved bottleneck in table extraction: appendices show perfect table match in only 7.1% of CHARTOM pairs, and extraction accuracy varies wildly by misleader type (0%-85.7%), but paper doesn't propose solutions for this critical component
Weak Experiment 2 (consistency assessment): only 4 visualization pairs tested; statistical significance only for truncated axis; findings are inconclusive and don't strongly support main claims

Practical applicability concerns: methods require knowing chart type in advance; redrawing unsupported for maps; no computational cost analysis; no clear guidance for practitioners on method selection; real-world scenarios with recent data lose parametric knowledge advantage

Limited investigation of why extracted axes (high accuracy, 20-25/30 correct) don't improve QA: MLLMs appear to ignore structured textual information and rely primarily on image, but this fundamental architectural issue isn't explored

CoT prompting shows only inconsistent modest gains, suggesting simple prompting approaches insufficient; axes extraction shows MLLMs ignore extracted information; together these suggest deeper architectural issues not addressed

strengths: Important and timely problem: Addresses critical vulnerability in deployed MLLMs relevant to disinformation concerns with clear societal implications
Comprehensive evaluation: 19 MLLMs, 17 misleader types, multiple datasets (synthetic and real-world), multiple evaluation dimensions beyond just accuracy
Rigorous methodology: Appropriate statistical tests, clear baselines including human performance, logical progression through three experiments, sound experimental design
Real-world contribution: Introduces new dataset of 42 real-world misleading visualizations with carefully constructed MCQs
Thorough analysis: Extensive appendices with qualitative error analysis, detailed breakdown by misleader type, manual analysis of specific failure modes with illustrative examples
Reproducibility: All prompts provided, implementation details clear, code and data promised for release, zero-shot evaluation setup clearly specified
Honest reporting: Candid discussion of limitations, trade-offs (e.g., table-based QA hurting non-misleading performance), bottlenecks, and unrealistic assumptions
Practical solutions: Two inference-time correction methods requiring no retraining, immediately actionable for practitioners
Insightful findings: Differences between human and MLLM vulnerabilities, parametric knowledge effects on real-world data, lack of correlation between ChartQA performance and misleading robustness
weaknesses: Dataset limitations: Only 143 misleading instances vs 2500 in ChartQA, severe class imbalance (truncated/inverted axes dominant, some categories with n=1), constrains statistical power and generalization despite reasonable justification

Limited solution effectiveness: Table extraction bottleneck varies dramatically by misleader (0% for dual axis), both effective methods depend on solving table extraction, no clear practical deployment path without solving this underlying problem first

Trade-offs inadequately addressed: Table-based QA reduces non-misleading performance (up to 8.5pp), redrawing fails for maps and complex charts (79-80% success), limitations undermine practical applicability
Experiment 2 underpowered: Only 4 visualization pairs, limited misleader types, significance found only for truncated axis, insufficient for robust conclusions about consistency
Experiment 3 scope restricted: Only 3/19 models tested despite others performing better, zero-shot only without exploring few-shot or prompting variants, temperature fixed at 0

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: Limited investigation into why certain misleaders affect MLLMs differently than humans (e.g., area encoding), parametric knowledge advantage only briefly analyzed, why combining visualization with extracted axes/tables fails when extractions are individually correct

Real-world applicability gaps: No evaluation of misleader detection methods (prerequisite for selective application), assumes prior knowledge of chart type, gap between laboratory QA task and deployment unclear, complex visualization types (maps, treemaps) not adequately addressed
Methodological concerns: No inter-annotator agreement reported for new 42-instance dataset, ground-truth misleader labels unrealistic for warning method, limited exploration of design space
Presentation issues: Figure 12 extremely crowded and difficult to interpret, key results sometimes buried in appendices, limited discussion of statistical significance upfront in main text

Limited solution breadth: No ensemble methods, no training-time approaches, no multi-modal fusion, Chain-of-Thought analysis relegated to appendix with mixed results, no exploration of alternative prompting strategies
